title: Fourier, Spectra and Distortion
intro: Harmonic distortion, spurs and spectra come from transient results. ngspice has four tools for them: .four and fourier for the harmonics of a periodic waveform and its THD, fft and spec for full spectra, psd for power spectral density, and the older small-signal .disto analysis. Getting clean numbers depends more on the time grid and the window than on the command.

blocks.source:
Harmonic distortion of a soft limiter
VIN in 0 SIN(0 1 1k)
Bnl out 0 V = tanh(V(in))
R1 out 0 1k
.control
  tran 1u 5m 0 1u
  fourier 1k v(out)          $ also as a dot command: .four 1k v(out)
  let h3 = fourier11[1][3] / fourier11[1][1]
  print h3
.endc
.end

blocks.text: fourier f0 vectors analyses the last period of the run (numPeriod since version 46 for more), interpolated onto a grid, and prints the magnitude and phase of the DC term and the first nine harmonics, normalised to the fundamental, plus the THD. Here the THD is 6.7% and the third harmonic 6.7% of the fundamental: tanh is odd, so the even harmonics are zero to numerical precision. The results are also stored as vectors (fourier11 and so on: rows are harmonic number, magnitude, phase, normalised values), unless set fournosave. set nfreqs=20 asks for more harmonics, and set fourgridsize the interpolation grid.

items: The run must be long enough to reach steady state, and the last period must be exact: let the simulation end on a whole number of periods after settling.
Accuracy depends on the time steps: give a tmax of a small fraction of the period (1/100 or less for a 0.1% THD figure), and tighten reltol (1e-4 or 1e-5) for distortion below about -80 dB.
With trap ringing in the waveform, high harmonics are garbage; see Transient Analysis.

blocks.source:
Spectrum of a two-tone signal through a cubic nonlinearity
VA a 0 SIN(0 0.5 10k)
VB b a SIN(0 0.5 11k)
Bnl out 0 V = V(b) - 0.1*V(b)*V(b)*V(b)
R1 out 0 1k
.control
  tran 0.5u 2m 0 0.5u
  linearize v(out)               $ fft needs equally spaced points
  set specwindow=blackman        $ hanning, hamming, blackman, flattop, gaussian, none ...
  fft v(out)                     $ makes a new plot (sp1) with frequency as scale
  meas sp p10k  find vdb(out) at=10k
  meas sp im3lo find vdb(out) at=9k
  let im3_dbc = im3lo - p10k
  print im3_dbc
.endc
.end

items: fft vectors: a windowed FFT of transient vectors; the result is a new plot of complex spectra. Resolution is 1/(simulated time): 2 ms gives 500 Hz bins here, enough to separate 9, 10, 11 and 12 kHz. Run long enough for the resolution you need.
The input must be on a uniform grid: run linearize (or set interp before the run) first. Without it ngspice interpolates for you and prints a note.

Windows: set specwindow to rectangular (none), bartlet, blackman, hanning, hamming, gaussian (with specwindoworder) or flattop. Blackman or Blackman-Harris for spurs far below the carrier, flattop for accurate amplitudes, none when the signal is exactly periodic in the window.
spec fstart fstop fstep vectors: a DFT on a frequency grid you choose (the step must be at least 1/(simulated time)).
psd smooth vectors: a single-sided power spectral density (the smooth argument averages adjacent bins), and it prints the total power up to the Nyquist frequency. Use it for transient-noise results.
ifft goes back from a spectrum to time.
Measurements on an fft plot use meas sp ... find ... at=...

blocks.text: In the two-tone run the third-order intermodulation product at 2 x 10 kHz - 11 kHz = 9 kHz comes out 36 dB below each tone (dBc). For the nonlinearity y = x - a x^3 with two tones of amplitude A, theory gives IM3 = (3/4) a A^3 against a fundamental of A, which is -36 dB for a = 0.1 and A = 0.5, less the small compression of the fundamental: close to what the fft shows.

blocks.source:
.disto of a BJT stage: second and third harmonic at the collector
.model qn NPN (is=1e-16 bf=100)
VCC vcc 0 5
VIN b 0 DC 0.7 AC 1 DISTOF1 0.01      $ 10 mV amplitude for the distortion analysis
RC vcc c 1k
Q1 c b 0 qn
.control
  disto dec 1 1k 10k
  setplot disto1                       $ 2nd harmonic
  print mag(v(c))
  setplot disto2                       $ 3rd harmonic
  print mag(v(c))
.endc
.end

blocks.text: .disto computes distortion by a Volterra-series expansion of the device nonlinearities around the operating point: harmonics HD2 and HD3 with one input frequency, and the intermodulation products when a second source has DISTOF2 and f2overf1 is given. It is fast and noise-free, but works only for the built-in semiconductor devices: B sources, XSPICE models and OSDI models contribute no distortion. For this stage it gives 2.1 mV of second harmonic and 0.14 mV of third, matching the exponential law (Ic (a^2/4) RC and Ic (a^3/24) RC with a = 10 mV / 26 mV). Prefer transient plus fourier when in doubt.

blocks.title: Frequency resolution
blocks.text: You need to see a spur 200 Hz away from a 1 MHz carrier. How long must the transient be, and what window?
solution: Resolution is 1/T. To resolve 200 Hz you need bins well below that, say 50 Hz, so T = 20 ms of steady-state data (after the start-up transient; use tstart to skip it).
A window with low sidelobes (Blackman or Blackman-Harris) keeps the carrier's leakage from burying the spur.
blocks.answer: About 20 ms of settled data, Blackman window.

blocks.title: THD from the vectors
blocks.text: How do you compute THD in dB from the fourier result instead of reading the printout?
solution: Use the stored vectors: with a vector fourier11 whose row 1 holds magnitudes for harmonics 0 to 9, THD = sqrt(sum over n = 2..9 of m_n^2) / m_1. In the control language: let m = fourier11[1]; let thd = sqrt(m[2]^2 + m[3]^2 + ... ) / m[1]; print db(thd).
blocks.answer: Square-sum the harmonic magnitudes from the fourier vector, divide by the fundamental.

items: H. Vogt, G. Atkinson, D. Warning and P. Nenzi, Ngspice User's Manual, version 47, 2026 (ngspice.sourceforge.io/docs.html), sections 11.3.3 (.disto), 11.6.4 (.four) and 13.5 (fourier, fft, spec, psd, linearize).
F. J. Harris, 'On the use of windows for harmonic analysis with the discrete Fourier transform,' Proc. IEEE, vol. 66, no. 1, 1978.
